questions.q:
(a) Depict graphically: Phased development methodology.

(b) During the Project Planning phase, the next cash flows were identified:

  • Development costs: Office space and equipment $45,000; Vendor installation $35,000; Data conversion tools $20,000
  • Operational costs: Software upgrades $15,000; Operational team salaries $20,000; User training $5,000
  • Tangible benefits: Increased sales $50,000; Reduction in staff $25,000; Better supplier prices $10,000

Find: ROI, BEP and NPV, if the project life cycle is 3 years and rate of return = 7%.
questions.a:
(a) Draw Planning and Analysis once, then 3 cycles (Analysis → Design → Implementation), each in a dotted ellipse and each ending in a rounded "System version n". A long arrow goes from each version into the Analysis of the next cycle. Add wavy back-arrows between boxes. Write: "The system is built as a series of versions; the most important requirements go into version 1. Pro: a useful system reaches users quickly. Con: users work with an intentionally incomplete system. RAD methodology."

(b) Assumption: development costs once in Year 0; operational costs and benefits every year, Years 1–3.

Development = 45,000 + 35,000 + 20,000 = 100,000. Operational = 15,000 + 20,000 + 5,000 = 40,000/yr. Benefits = 50,000 + 25,000 + 10,000 = 85,000/yr.

Year 0Year 1Year 2Year 3Total
Total Benefits085,00085,00085,000255,000
Total Costs100,00040,00040,00040,000220,000
Net Benefits(100,000)45,00045,00045,00035,000
Cumulative(100,000)(55,000)(10,000)35,000
Divide by 1.07n11.071.14491.225043
PV of Benefits079,439.2574,242.2969,385.32223,066.86
PV of Costs100,000.0037,383.1834,937.5532,651.92204,972.64

ROI = (255,000 − 220,000) / 220,000 = 35,000 / 220,000 = 15.91%

BEP: cumulative turns positive in Year 3; negative years before it (not counting Year 0) = 2. BEP = 2 + (45,000 − 35,000) / 45,000 = 2 + 0.22 = 2.22 years.

NPV = 223,066.86 − 204,972.64 = $18,094.22 > 0 → economically acceptable.

questions.q:
A student solved Quiz 1 Version 2 (development $110,000 incl. Data conversion tools $20,000; operational $40,000/yr; benefits $110,000/yr; 10%) and wrote these three lines. Find the mistake in each and give the correct result.

  1. "Development = 40,000 + 50,000 + 20,000 + User training 10,000 = 120,000."
  2. "PV of Year 0 cost = 110,000 / 1.10 = 100,000."
  3. "Cumulative: (110,000), (40,000), 30,000. Years 0 and 1 are negative, so BEP = 2 + (70,000 − 30,000) / 70,000 = 2.57 years."
questions.a:
1. User training is an operational cost (every year), not development. Development = 40,000 + 50,000 + 20,000 = 110,000.
  2. Year 0 is not discounted ((1 + r)0 = 1). PV of Year 0 cost = 110,000.
  3. Year 0 is not counted as a negative year. Only Year 1 counts: BEP = 1 + 40,000 / 70,000 = 1.57 years.

With these fixes: ROI = 43.48%, NPV = $64,079.64 > 0 → acceptable.

questions.q:
For the same project, the rate of return in the question changes from 7% to 18%. All cash flows stay the same. Which results change?

A) ROI, BEP and NPV
B) Only ROI
C) Only NPV
D) BEP and NPV
questions.a: C, because only NPV uses the rate (it discounts future money). ROI and BEP use the undiscounted table, so they do not change. A higher rate makes the NPV smaller.

questions.q:
In which stage of the project management process does the manager develop a risk management strategy?

A) Initiation
B) Planning
C) Execution
D) Monitoring and Controlling
questions.a: B, because Planning = create the project plan, create the WBS and develop a risk management strategy. (Initiation creates the project charter.)

questions.q: The university library wants a mobile app so students can reserve books and study rooms. It needs 3 developers, costs about $25,000, takes 4 months, and is used only by the library department. The team has built similar apps before. The library expects to save staff time at the front desk. Classify this project using the 7 ways.
questions.a:
• Size: small, 3 people.
  • Cost: $25,000 (low).
  • Purpose: improve operations (less front-desk work, better service).
  • Length: 4 months; value comes when the app goes live.
  • Risk: low, the team has built similar apps.
  • Scope: one department (the library), not the whole university.
  • ROI: compare the saved staff time (in money) with the $25,000.

A) Work breakdown structure
B) Gantt chart

questions.a: D, because the 3 traditional tools are the WBS, the Gantt chart and the network diagram (PERT/CPM). A use case diagram is an analysis-phase model, not a PM tool.

questions.q:
On a network diagram, task 6 is drawn with crossed lines (an X) and task 9 with one diagonal line. What does this mean?

A) 6 is critical, 9 is not critical
B) 6 is completed, 9 is partially completed
C) 6 is cancelled, 9 is delayed
D) 6 is a milestone, 9 is a dependency
questions.a: B, because one diagonal line = partially completed and crossed lines = completed. Critical tasks are shown with a special (double) border, milestones are diamonds or upside-down triangles on a Gantt chart.

questions.q: Compare the Gantt chart and the network diagram: what does each show best, and where do both get their data from?
questions.a:
• Gantt chart: a horizontal bar chart; tasks are rows, time runs across the top. Best for time: when each task starts and ends, progress (filled bars), milestones (◆/▼), who is assigned. Shows high-level status quickly.
  • Network diagram: a node-and-arc graph; nodes = tasks with time estimates, arcs = dependencies. Best for dependencies and finding the critical path (CPM, with or without PERT).
  • Both are driven by the WBS (tasks, durations, status, dependencies).

questions.q: At the end of inception, a well-done project plan estimates a new hospital appointment system at $120,000 and 16 weeks. Using the hurricane model, give the realistic ranges for cost and schedule. How should these ranges change later in the project?
questions.a:
Hurricane model: ±100% for cost, ±25% for schedule at the end of inception.

Cost: 120,000 ± 120,000 = $0 to $240,000.

Schedule: 16 ± 0.25 × 16 = 16 ± 4 = 12 to 20 weeks.

The ranges get narrower through Elaboration, Construction and Transition, as the system becomes better defined.

questions.q: A project was planned for 24 weeks. Analysis was planned for 6 weeks but took 8. The remaining work is planned for 18 weeks. Give the new end week under each of the three actions, and the risk of each.
questions.a:
ActionWorkingNew endRisk
Do not change the scheduleassume you make up the 2 weeksweek 24High
Add the time you are behind24 + 2week 26Moderate
Add the same percentage% = 2 ÷ 6 (planned) = 33.3%; 18 × 1.333 = 24; 8 + 24week 32Low

If the sponsor cannot accept week 32, reduce the scope. Trap: the % uses the planned 6 weeks, not the actual 8.

questions.q:
Which is NOT one of the three underlying problems of traditional work breakdown structures?

A) They focus on the design of the system and force premature decomposition
B) They have too many or too few levels of detail
C) They are project-specific and hard to compare across projects
D) They cannot show task dependencies
questions.a: D, because a WBS must show dependencies (with duration and status). The 3 problems are design focus, wrong level of detail, and being hard to compare across projects.

questions.q: In a 20-week project, the design phase finishes 2 weeks early. The team leader wants to tell the sponsor "we will now finish in week 18". What should the project manager do instead, and why?
questions.a: Move the next deadlines 2 weeks sooner, but do not change the promised completion date (keep week 20). Estimates early in a project are still uncertain (hurricane model), so the saved time is a buffer for later problems. Also record the actual time so future estimates are better.

questions.q: The sponsor of a café ordering app says: "Deliver 4 weeks earlier, same budget." Using the idea of project trade-offs, explain what the project manager can offer.
questions.a: Project management is making trade-offs among functionality, time and cost. If time goes down and cost stays the same, functionality must go down: deliver the core (menu, order, pay) on the earlier date and postpone extras (loyalty card) to a later version. The other option is to keep all functionality and raise the cost, but adding people to a project does not always increase productivity.

questions.q: A hospital appointment system is half built. Three new requests arrive: (1) the head doctor saw the prototype and now wants online video visits; (2) a developer wants to add a voice assistant because he finds it interesting; (3) the director wants the system to support a new partnership strategy announced at a board meeting. Name the problem, its source in each case, and what the project manager should do.
questions.a:
This is scope creep: new requirements added after the scope was defined and frozen, the most common reason for schedule and cost overruns.

  • (1) Users see the system's potential and want new functions.
  • (2) Developers get attached to an interesting capability.
  • (3) A senior manager adds a new strategy.

Actions: carefully examine the impact of each change; allow only changes that are absolutely necessary; delay the rest as future enhancements (e.g. video visits in version 2); or use timeboxing.

questions.q: Depict graphically: timeboxing for a university festival app that must be ready on 1 March. Wanted features: registration, event schedule, campus map, chat.
questions.a: Draw the 6 steps as a flow with a loop: 1 set the delivery date (1 March) → 2 prioritize functionality → 3 build the core (registration and schedule) → 4 postpone what cannot be done in time (map, chat) → 5 deliver with core functionality → 6 repeat steps 3–5 to add refinements. Note: timeboxing is time-oriented; it places meeting the deadline above delivering all functionality.

questions.q:
A tester reports in JIRA: "The Pay button does nothing on iPhone." Which issue type should this be?

A) Epic
B) Story
C) Sub-Task
D) Bug
questions.a: D, because a Bug is "a problem that impairs or prevents the functions of the product". An Epic is a big user story to break down; a Story is a user story; a Sub-Task is a smaller piece of an issue.

questions.q: Classify each case by its cause of risk (weak personnel, scope creep, poor design, overly optimistic estimates): (a) the schedule assumed no one would ever be sick; (b) the client keeps adding new reports every week; (c) the team has never built a mobile app; (d) the database was designed without thinking about growth, and the system becomes very slow.
questions.a:
• (a) Overly optimistic estimates
  • (b) Scope creep
  • (c) Weak personnel
  • (d) Poor design

questions.q:
Which statement about timeboxing is correct?

A) It is task-oriented: more tasks make the project longer
B) It places meeting a deadline above delivering functionality
C) It delivers all functionality before the deadline is set
D) It is used only to estimate costs
questions.a: B, because timeboxing is a time-oriented approach to scope management: set the date first, build the core, and postpone what does not fit.
